findings.evidence:
export const bucket = (ps: Price[]) =>
  ps.reduce<Record<string, Price[]>>((a, p) => ((a[(p.cents >> 4) & 0x3e8 ? "hi" : "lo"] ||= []).push(p), a), {});
findings.recommendation: A reader cannot tell from this line what makes a price premium: the rule "10 euros and more" (1000 cents, from the proposal) is hidden behind a shift and a bitmask, `(p.cents >> 4) & 0x3e8`, which reads like a threshold of 1000 but is not a comparison at all. The shape hides a wrong result: a 500-cent price gives `31 & 1000 = 8`, truthy, so it lands in "hi", while the docstring promises cheap vs premium. The comma expression inside `reduce`, the `||=` side effect, the one-letter names (`ps`, `a`, `p`), the `hi`/`lo` keys that do not match "cheap"/"premium", and the untyped `Record<string, ...>` return add to it. Write the simple version: a named constant `PREMIUM_THRESHOLD_CENTS = 1000`, a plain loop or two `filter` calls comparing `price.cents >= PREMIUM_THRESHOLD_CENTS`, and a return type `{ cheap: Price[]; premium: Price[] }` — fixing the misclassification is the developer's call, as it changes behavior.
findings.title: `bucket` packs the premium rule into an unreadable bit-trick one-liner
